Lean, vectorbt/vectorbt.pro, ABIDES, mbt_gym, backtrader, zipline-reloaded, hummingbot and freqtrade were screened by the coordinator against this task's requirements (native per-order latency model, L1 queue/liquidity realism, a native per-account rate limiter, Python strategy API) and found unsuitable for the reasons in decision_and_scope.scope and this record's limitations.
license_and_compatibility: NautilusTrader is LGPL-3.0 (already the accepted north-star engine license posture); hftbacktest is MIT. No new native authentication, credential export or model default follows from this record.

predeclared_metrics.quality_rule: The elite-tier profile must sustain >=180 fills/simulated-minute in every full minute of the 30-minute analysis window, independently recounted from NautilusTrader's own generate_fills_report() and matching the strategy's own counters exactly; the paper-parity profile must never exceed 180 fills/min (by construction of its RiskEngineConfig budget). Both must flatten to zero net position at end.
predeclared_metrics.usage_rule: No token/model usage is claimed by this record (usage_assessment.claim is 'none'); this is an infrastructure capacity measurement, not a model-task comparison.

failures_and_skips.reason: Use-after-free in run_hftbacktest.py (a per-symbol numpy feed array was reassigned out of scope inside the asset-build loop, silently freeing hftbacktest's only backing memory for the first-built symbol's data while the Rust side kept a raw pointer into it) produced non-deterministic, corrupted hftbacktest output. This corruption drove the entire withdrawn F1/F2 narrative in the superseded receipt (a reported ~82% NVDA fill-rate divergence and a spurious PartialFillExchange-vs-NoPartialFillExchange disagreement), refuted by an independent adversarial review and independently reproduced by this task (see the superseded receipt's superseded_first_attempt block for hashes and the full root-cause citation). Superseded by engine-vs-engine-crosscheck-20260925-repair, which fixes the driver and reaches the opposite conclusion: the two engines agree within tolerance and sim-capacity's NautilusTrader destination is not overturned.

task_and_failure: The simulation lane needed evidence of a synthetic, fixture-scoped fill-throughput ceiling under a native per-account rate limiter (deliberately made to bind, not left non-binding, so it cannot be misread as a broker-throughput statement), a primary-reference (not calibrated) latency setting, and quotes-only L1 execution -- specifically, whether >=180 fills/simulated-minute is achievable in a fixture with no strategy manufacturing a trade to hit that number. This is infrastructure capacity evidence, never strategy performance and never a broker-throughput claim (see NS-06 in limitations).

limitations: Lean has no per-order latency model and fills whole orders against a bar, not a native queue/liquidity model, so it cannot exercise a submit-rate limiter's interaction with fine-grained fill timing the way this test needs.
vectorbt and vectorbt.pro are bar-level (no tick-level order lifecycle, no native rate limiter), unsuitable for a per-order-submission capacity test.
ABIDES is archived with old, hard-to-reproduce dependencies and synthetic-only agents; not selected for a real-data capacity replay.
mbt_gym targets RL environment design, not a broker-realistic order/fill/fee pipeline.
backtrader and zipline-reloaded lack a native per-order latency model and a per-account rate limiter comparable to a real broker's.
hummingbot and freqtrade are crypto-market execution frameworks; their fee/queue/latency assumptions do not match US equities or Alpaca's REST rate-limit semantics.
MarS is GPU-hosted and trained on Chinese-market data; out of scope for a US-equities Alpaca capacity test with no GPU dependency in this lane.
hftbacktest was not run as a cross-check in this record (next-phase item; see next_decision_changing_test) -- it remains a comparison harness on a tick subset only per mover-v3/README.md.

This is infrastructure capacity evidence only: no order reacts to a signal, and no strategy manufactures a trade to hit a throughput target (docs/harness-rules-convergence-20260922.md NS-06; blueprints/us-equities/adaptive-paper/README.md L41).

An independent review found 41.2% of elite-tier fills beat the NBBO touch when trade ticks were fed into the engine alongside quotes (an rc5 L1-book artifact: a trade print overwrites both sides of the book and nothing restores the prior quote for a NO_AGGRESSOR trade). Fixed by feeding quotes only into the engine (trade ticks are still fetched and cataloged for future passive-order work, just not replayed here); measured 0 touch violations after the fix, asserted by cmd_run in every run including the latency sweep, and cross-checked by the builder with the reviewer's own harness before commit (the reviewer separately verifies independently).

An independent review found 162/163 elite and 112/113 paper order rejects were 'Short selling not permitted on a CASH account', consuming rate-limit budget and driving position-cap skips. Fixed with inventory-aware side selection (never sell from a flat or short position; a sell's quantity is clamped to the current long); measured 0 short-sale rejects after the fix.

Alpaca's historical trade data carries no aggressor-side field; every TradeTick is tagged NO_AGGRESSOR, which makes any queue-depletion-based fill estimate derived from these trade ticks optimistic (documented in fetcher.py).

The FINRA TAF cap's per-order-vs-per-execution scope is now settled for this exerciser (FINRA TAF FAQ A200.17, verbatim: a member may calculate the fee on 'either the individual street side executions or ... the account level average price confirmation', an average-price-allocation choice this exerciser's plain per-fill IOC activity does not involve, so the street-side-execution/per-fill method applies); this fee model already applies it per fill, which is the settled, sourced behavior for this case (documented in fee_model.py).

Undocumented rc5 behavior: a book level's consumed-quantity tally under liquidity_consumption=True resets only when that price's displayed size actually changes (matching_engine/mod.rs:371-375), clearing otherwise only on a book reset or instrument precision change (:297-298,:1338-1339) -- an identical repeated (price, size) quote never replenishes liquidity between them. Measured on the committed elite-tier@70ms receipt: 66 of 855 IOC expiries (~0.25% of the 26,155 total fills) are marketable-at-cancel with nonzero displayed size, already consumed by an earlier fill at that same (symbol, side, price) since the quote instance in force first appeared. This makes the lane's throughput/cost figures pessimistic (fewer fills), not inflated. It also broke an early, unmodified-quote test fixture (4 fills, then 95-99% expiry for the rest of the run); the shared fixture now varies displayed size tick-to-tick so liquidity keeps replenishing.

2026-09-25 dated cross-check result (blueprints/us-equities/sim-engine-crosscheck/, evidence_class sim_engine_crosscheck): hftbacktest 2.4.4 diverges from this experiment's NautilusTrader fill rate by more than 20% (28.55% at 70ms, 27.20% at 250ms, on a shared deterministic order stream over a bounded SPY+NVDA sample), triggering this record's overturn condition -- but median time-to-fill stays within the 2x threshold at both latencies, and the fill-rate divergence is attributed to a documented model-semantics difference (NautilusTrader's latency-release-on-next-quote-or-timer semantics vs hftbacktest's literal constant order latency, interacting with NVDA's sparser/gappier quotes -- SPY alone is within -0.28% at 70ms), not a matching bug, so the NautilusTrader destination is NOT overturned by this result. A separate, smaller effect (hftbacktest's own PartialFillExchange vs NoPartialFillExchange disagreeing on NVDA at 70ms only, vanishing at 250ms) is flagged in that receipt as a suspected hftbacktest-internal inconsistency, not filed upstream, and is too small to itself explain the >20% divergence.

2026-09-25 repair-round correction of the entry immediately above: an independent adversarial review found and this task independently reproduced a use-after-free in the cross-check's own run_hftbacktest.py driver (a per-symbol numpy feed array losing its only Python reference mid-loop while hftbacktest held a raw, non-owning pointer into it), which had corrupted every hftbacktest result the prior entry described. Both withdrawn findings (F1's ~82% NVDA fill-rate divergence and F2's PartialFillExchange/NoPartialFillExchange disagreement) were artifacts of that corruption, not real engine behavior. With the driver fixed (verified via a determinism rerun and a two-symbol-vs-single-symbol isolation check, both hash-identical; see blueprints/us-equities/sim-engine-crosscheck/receipts/20260925-crosscheck.json), NautilusTrader and hftbacktest agree within 0.30-0.36% fill rate and 1.16-1.59x median time-to-fill (1.0x on a NautilusTrader exact-latency variant added this round) -- the >20%/2x overturn condition is NOT triggered, and the NautilusTrader destination is NOT overturned. A separate, minor, real NautilusTrader timing property was also found and reported (a deferred order releases only at its own instrument's next quote or any due timer, not exactly at submit+latency; measured extra delay median ~29ms SPY / ~58ms NVDA, p90 ~136/263ms), with a fix for sim-capacity's own exerciser recommended as a separate follow-up PR, not made here.
